issues.legal_issue: A state legislature may enact a law extinguishing private rights in mines, minerals, and quarries without legislating in the field reserved for central regulation of their development.
material_facts: An earlier judicial interpretation had left mineral rights in certain granted lands outside the operation of the land-tenure abolition law.

The challenged law extinguished existing rights in mines, minerals, and quarries in land and vested those rights in the State, while making their regulation and development subject to central legislation.
issues.conclusion: The law was within the State Legislature’s competence and was not invalid for encroaching on the central field of regulation and development of mines and minerals.
issues.legal_principle: Legislative entries are fields of legislation, not independent sources of power; under Article 246 they are construed broadly, and an enactment is classified by its pith and substance. The Court relied on India Cement Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu for these principles, but distinguished it because the challenged law acquired and vested mineral rights rather than imposing a tax on royalty. It also distinguished Orissa Cement Ltd. v. State of Orissa and Federation of Mining Associations of Rajasthan v. State of Rajasthan. The law was supported by Entries 18 and 23 of List II and Entry 42 of List III, subject to Entry 54 of List I.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_state_law: A litigant challenged the constitutional validity of a state law.
predicates.law_extinguishes_private_mineral_rights: The state law extinguished private rights in minerals or quarries situated in land and vested those rights in the State.
predicates.mineral_regulation_remains_subject_to_ce: The law left the regulation and development of mines and minerals subject to the applicable central regime.

issues.definition: When a challenged state law acquires private mineral rights while leaving mineral regulation to the central regime, the State Legislature has competence to enact it.

issues.legal_issue: A law governing mineral rights in granted land may apply despite earlier special land-tenure enactments that were not separately amended.
material_facts: Earlier enactments abolished particular land tenures and dealt with the rights of former landholders and cultivators.
The later law applied to mines, minerals, and quarries in land held under grants, agreements, or court orders, including land held by former tenure holders.
The later law contained overriding language and operated from the date the State was formed.
issues.conclusion: The law applied to mineral rights in the land and was not rendered inoperative because the earlier special enactments had not been amended.
issues.legal_principle: The earlier enactments dealt with the abolition of land tenures and the related rights in land, whereas the later provisions specifically covered mineral rights in granted or otherwise recognized land. The overriding language of the later provisions brought those rights within the State’s reservation and vesting scheme. The argument that the earlier special laws prevailed over the general revenue law therefore failed.

predicates.challenge_to_later_state_law: A litigant challenged whether a later state law applied to rights arising under earlier land-tenure enactments.
predicates.earlier_tenure_laws_exist: Earlier enactments governed the abolition of land tenures and related landholder and cultivator rights.
predicates.later_law_expressly_covers_mineral_right: The later law expressly covered mineral rights in land held under grants, agreements, or court orders.

issues.definition: When earlier tenure laws exist but a later law expressly covers mineral rights in granted land, the later law applies to those rights.

issues.legal_issue: A legislature may give a law retrospective effect from the date on which the State Legislature acquired authority to legislate.
material_facts: The challenged law expressly operated from the date the State was formed, although it was enacted later.
The law retrospectively affected rights previously claimed under grants, agreements, or judicial decisions.
issues.conclusion: The retrospective operation was valid and did not make the law ultra vires.
issues.legal_principle: Unless constitutionally prohibited, legislative power includes the power to legislate retrospectively. The Court relied on Tata Iron and Steel Co. v. State of Bihar and Rama Krishna v. State of Bihar. It held that the express retrospective effect was tied to the date on which the State came into existence and its legislature became competent to enact the law.

predicates.challenge_to_retroactive_state_law: A litigant challenged the retrospective operation of a state law.
predicates.law_expressly_operates_from_state_legisl: The law expressly states that it operates from the point at which the State Legislature acquired authority to enact it.
predicates.state_legislature_had_authority_from_tha: The State Legislature had legislative authority from the point selected for the law’s retrospective operation.

issues.definition: A challenged state law may operate retrospectively from the point when the State Legislature acquired authority to enact it.

issues.legal_issue: A law extinguishing landholder rights in the course of agrarian reform and distributing material resources does not violate the Constitution’s basic structure or fundamental-rights guarantees when protected by the applicable constitutional provisions.
material_facts: The law extinguished former landholders’ interests in land and mineral resources as part of a broader scheme of land-tenure abolition and agrarian reform.
The law was included in the Ninth Schedule and was directed to vesting resources in the State for public use.
The claimants argued that the law violated constitutional protections, including equality and the right to property, and damaged the Constitution’s basic structure.
issues.conclusion: The law was protected as part of agrarian reform and did not damage the Constitution’s basic structure; it was also saved by the constitutional protection for laws giving effect to the distribution of material resources for the common good.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Articles 31A, 31B, and 31C, and Articles 39(b) and 39(c), together with the Ninth Schedule. It held that land and embedded mines, minerals, and quarries are material resources of the community, and that their acquisition can be a means of distributing those resources for the common good. It also held that the right to property under Article 300A is not a basic feature or structure of the Constitution. The Court relied on Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, Waman Rao v. Union of India, State of Tamil Nadu v. L. Abu Kavibai, Sanjeev Coke Manufacturing Co. v. Bharat Cooking Coal Ltd., and other decisions concerning agrarian reform, material resources, and constitutional structure.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_law and law_forms_part_of_agrarian_reform and law_distributes_community_resources and law_has_constitutional_protection

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_: A litigant challenged the constitutional validity of a law affecting land rights.
predicates.law_forms_part_of_agrarian_reform: The law forms part of a scheme that abolishes intermediary land tenures or reorganizes land rights.
predicates.law_distributes_community_resources: The law vests or distributes land or embedded natural resources for public use or the common good.
predicates.law_has_constitutional_protection: The law falls within a constitutional protection for agrarian reform or laws directed to distributing material resources for the common good.

issues.definition: A challenged law that forms part of agrarian reform, distributes community resources, and has constitutional protection does not damage the Constitution’s basic structure.

issues.legal_issue: Private property may be acquired for a public purpose under authority of law without a constitutional requirement to pay market value or a just equivalent.
material_facts: The law vested privately held rights in mines, minerals, and quarries in the State.
The acquisition was made by legislation and formed part of a scheme to place mineral resources under State control for public use.
The claimants argued that the deprivation was invalid because the law did not provide market-value compensation or a just equivalent.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition was valid under Article 300A, and payment of market value or a just equivalent was not a necessary condition of that deprivation.
issues.legal_principle: Article 300A requires deprivation of property to be authorized by law; it does not restore the former constitutional requirement of compensation under Article 31(2), which was omitted. Acquisition under the sovereign power of eminent domain must be for a public purpose, but the amount need not equal market value. The Court relied on Chiranjit Lal Chowdhuri v. Union of India, State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh, Bisambhar Dayal Chandra Mohan v. State of U.P., and the constitutional history surrounding the omission of Article 31(2). It also explained that property includes rights in mines, minerals, and quarries.

predicates.challenge_to_property_acquisition: A litigant challenged the State’s acquisition or taking of private property.
predicates.deprivation_is_authorized_by_law: The deprivation was carried out under an enactment or other law having force of law, rather than by executive fiat.
predicates.acquisition_serves_public_purpose: The acquired property or rights were taken for a public purpose.

issues.definition: A challenged property acquisition authorized by law for a public purpose may be valid without payment of a market equivalent.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory principle for determining an acquisition amount is valid if it is relevant to the acquisition and is not illusory, even though the resulting amount need not be adequate.
material_facts: The law provided for an amount based on the average net annual income received from the relevant mineral products before vesting.
The claimants argued that the amount was not equivalent to the value of the rights taken and was illusory.
The Court found the income-based principle relevant to determining the amount and the resulting amount not illusory.
issues.conclusion: The statutory principle for determining the amount was valid; its adequacy could not be challenged in court.
issues.legal_principle: After the constitutional changes that removed the former compensation guarantee, courts may review whether the principles used to determine an acquisition amount are relevant and whether the amount is illusory, but they may not review adequacy. The Court relied on Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, Bhim Singhji v. Union of India, Achutananda Purohit v. State of Orissa, State of Maharashtra v. Basantibai Mohanlal Khetan, and Tinsukhia Electric Supply Co. Ltd. v. State of Assam.

rule.if: challenge_to_acquisition_amount and amount_uses_property_related_income_principle and principle_is_relevant and amount_is_not_illusory

predicates.challenge_to_acquisition_amount: A litigant challenged the principle used to determine the amount payable for acquired property.
predicates.amount_uses_property_related_income_prin: The amount is determined by reference to income derived from the property or resource before it was taken.
predicates.principle_is_relevant: The chosen principle has a rational connection to determining the amount payable for the property or resource.
predicates.amount_is_not_illusory: The amount produced by the principle is not merely nominal or illusory.

issues.definition: A challenged acquisition-amount principle is valid when it relates to the property’s income and does not produce an illusory amount.

issues.legal_issue: Erosion in the value of money between vesting and payment does not invalidate an acquisition amount determined by a statutory principle.
material_facts: The amount was calculated by reference to income before the date on which the rights vested.
The claimants argued that inflation had reduced the purchasing power of the amount by the time it would be paid.
issues.conclusion: The erosion in the value of money did not invalidate the statutory principle or make the amount illusory.
issues.legal_principle: The loss of purchasing power caused by inflation is not, by itself, a ground for invalidating a statutory acquisition-amount principle. The Court relied on Achutananda Purohit v. State of Orissa and the principle that currency depreciation does not determine the validity of a statutory valuation method.

predicates.challenge_to_acquisition_amount: A litigant challenged the principle used to determine the amount payable for acquired property.
predicates.payment_follows_vesting: The amount is payable after the property or rights have vested in the State.
predicates.currency_value_has_declined: The purchasing power of the currency has declined between vesting and payment.

issues.definition: A decline in currency value after vesting does not invalidate an acquisition amount determined under a statutory principle.

issues.legal_issue: Different statutory methods for determining acquisition amounts do not establish discrimination or unfair procedure when the method in the challenged law is rationally related to its object.
material_facts: Other land and acquisition enactments used different methods to determine amounts payable for acquired property.
The challenged law used a principle based on prior net income from the mineral products.
The Court found that principle reasonably related to the modification and extinguishment of the existing rights.
issues.conclusion: The difference between statutory methods did not violate equality, and the claim of unfair procedure under Article 21 did not invalidate the acquisition.
issues.legal_principle: Comparison with the amount-determination methods in other enactments does not, by itself, establish discrimination. A method that bears a reasonable relation to the law’s object is not invalid merely because another statute uses a different method. The Court also held that the claim of unfair procedure under Article 21 did not apply to this deprivation of property. It relied on State of Maharashtra v. Basantibai Mohanlal Khetan, Tinsukhia Electric Supply Co. Ltd. v. State of Assam, and other decisions concerning statutory acquisition amounts and equality.

predicates.challenge_to_acquisition_amount: A litigant challenged the method used to determine the amount payable for acquired property.
predicates.claimant_compares_different_statutory_me: The litigant relied on different amount-determination methods used in other enactments as a basis for the challenge.
predicates.challenged_method_relates_to_law_object: The method used in the challenged law has a rational connection to the law’s object.

issues.definition: Comparing statutory amount-determination methods does not establish discrimination or unfairness when the challenged method relates to the law’s object.
